name: ci

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  smoke:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - name: Syntax-check every .cjs / .js
        run: |
          shopt -s globstar nullglob
          for f in **/*.cjs **/*.js; do
            case "$f" in node_modules/*) continue;; esac
            node --check "$f"
          done
      - name: Install (no secrets required)
        run: npm install --no-audit --no-fund || true
      - name: Test (runs against the zero-dependency echo path)
        run: npm test

--- ## Why LLM Split When two inference plans coexist, volume drifts toward whichever one the last refactor favored — and you discover it at invoice time. LLM Split makes the ratio a held invariant instead of an accident. The mechanism is deliberately small: a daily ledger file counts calls per side; record(side) is called at the two or three places in your codebase where calls actually leave (client choke points, so every caller is counted without touching call sites); and pickSide() implements one rule — if the second side's share is below target, route there; otherwise route to the first. Cold start seeds the flat-rate side first, so the metered plan is never the default by accident. Because the balancer only needs directional truth, it uses lock-free read-modify-write and stays out of your hot path entirely: no network, no dependencies, microseconds per call. status() gives you the live percentages and what the next pick would be — one command to see whether reality matches intent. --- ## What it does | Module | What it does | Signal | |---|---|---| | **ledger** | Daily counts per side in one JSON file — atomic tmp+rename writes, last 14 days kept, self-pruning | one small file, full fleet visibility | | **record(side)** | Count one call on a side; s.record('metered'); s.record('flat'); console.log(s.status())" # 4. route the next eligible call node -e "console.log(require('./lib/llm-split.cjs').pickSide())" # 5. retune the target (min % share for side B), or kill the split LLM_SPLIT_TARGET=35 node lib/llm-split.cjs LLM_SPLIT=0 node lib/llm-split.cjs ``` > Sides are names you choose (default: metered, flat) via LLM_SPLIT_SIDES. # LLM Split — Architecture

LLM Split solves a mundane, expensive problem: you have two ways to run inference — a metered API and a flat-rate plan, two subscriptions, two accounts — and you want the fleet's volume held to a deliberate ratio instead of drifting wherever habit takes it. Instrument your client choke points with record(side), and every call in the fleet is counted into a daily ledger regardless of which script made it. When a caller can go either way, pickSide() answers with the side currently under its target share. The target is one env var; the ledger is one small JSON file that keeps 14 days and writes atomically. It is a balancer, not a billing meter — counts are approximate under concurrent writers by design, which is exactly the tolerance a router needs. A kill switch reverts the fleet to single-provider behavior instantly.

## Flow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["any caller in the fleet"] --> CP["client choke point"]
    CP --> REC["record(side)\n→ daily ledger (atomic, 14d)"]
    Q["next call — which side?"] --> PS{"pickSide()\nside B share < target?"}
    PS -->|yes| B["side B (flat-rate plan)"]
    PS -->|no| M["side A (metered)"]
    REC -.-> PS
    S["status()"] -.->|counts · pcts · target · next| OBS["one-command observability"]
    classDef acc fill:#2c1f3d,stroke:#A06CE0,color:#fff;
    class PS acc;
    class REC acc;
```

## How it fits together

LLM Split is one pure-Node module around one small file. The ledger ({ "YYYY-MM-DD": { sideA: N, sideB: N } }) lives at data/ledger.json; save() sorts keys, keeps the newest 14 days, and writes via tmp-file + rename so a crash never leaves a torn file. Side names resolve from LLM_SPLIT_SIDES (default metered,flat) — side A is the metered/default side, side B the flat-rate side the target protects. record(side, n) validates the side name, loads, increments today's counter, and saves; it is wrapped so no filesystem failure ever propagates into an LLM call, and its read-modify-write is deliberately lock-free — under concurrent writers counts are approximate, which is the correct tolerance for a balancer and the documented wrong tool for billing. pickSide() implements the entire routing policy: disabled → side A; zero volume today → side B (cold start seeds the flat-rate plan first so the metered side is never the accidental default); otherwise side B while its percentage share is under LLM_SPLIT_TARGET, side A after. status() returns date, enabled, target, per-side counts and percentages, and the next pick; the CLI prints it as JSON. Integration is two lines at each client choke point (record after a successful call) plus pickSide() wherever a caller is genuinely side-agnostic.

## Extending it

Every capability is a self-contained module. To add your own, follow the contract the existing
modules use and wire it into the entry point. Keep it portable — config via `.env`, no hardcoded
paths, no personal accounts.

## Design principles

1. **A ratio is policy — hold it as one.** The split is a named target in config, converged on daily, not an accident of habit.
2. **Instrument choke points, not call sites.** Count where calls leave the building; every caller is covered without a fleet-wide refactor.
3. **A balancer, not a billing meter.** Lock-free approximate counts are the right tolerance for routing; invoices come from the provider.
4. **Never in the hot path.** No network, no locks, no dependencies; a counting failure never becomes a call failure.

what it does

A held ratio, not a hope.

01 / COUNT

Choke points, not call sites

Put record(side) inside the two or three client functions that calls actually flow through, and the entire fleet is counted — every script, every cron, every agent — without touching a single call site. The write is atomic, the file self-prunes to 14 days, and a failure to count never becomes a failure to call.

02 / ROUTE

One rule, held daily

pickSide() compares today's share against the target: under-target side wins the next call. The target is an env var you can retune any day — 50/50, 80/20, whatever the plans justify — and the split converges toward it as volume flows, without any coordinator process.

03 / OBSERVE

Intent vs reality in one command

node lib/llm-split.cjs prints the live status: today's counts, the percentage each side actually carried, the target, and which side the next call would ride. When the number drifts from the plan, you see it the same day — not on the invoice.

quickstart

Up and running in a clone.

Every value comes from .env. Nothing here is tied to any account — bring your own.

# 1. watch the split converge on a simulated 200-call day (no API key)
node examples/demo.cjs

# 2. live status — counts, percentages, target, and the next pick
node lib/llm-split.cjs

# 3. count calls from your client choke points
node -e "const s=require('./lib/llm-split.cjs'); s.record('metered'); s.record('flat'); console.log(s.status())"

# 4. route the next eligible call
node -e "console.log(require('./lib/llm-split.cjs').pickSide())"

# 5. retune the target (min % share for side B), or kill the split
LLM_SPLIT_TARGET=35 node lib/llm-split.cjs
LLM_SPLIT=0 node lib/llm-split.cjs
